title: Supreme Court Rules Live-In Partners Can Seek Cruelty Protection Under Section 498A
excerpt: The ruling expands the scope of India's anti-cruelty law beyond formally married couples, holding that the term 'husband' must be interpreted to include men in relationships resembling marriage.
body:
• The Supreme Court has ruled that women in live-in relationships resembling marriage can invoke Section 498A IPC against partners for cruelty, extending protections previously limited to legally wedded wives.
  • The bench held that the term "husband" under Section 498A must be given a purposive and expansive interpretation, focusing on the substance of a relationship rather than its formal legal validity.
  • The ruling upholds a November 2025 Karnataka High Court judgment in the case of Lokesh B.H. v. State of Karnataka, where a man was accused of harassment and attempted burning of his live-in partner.
  • Legal experts say the decision could reshape how Indian courts handle domestic violence complaints from the growing number of couples in live-in arrangements across the country.

The Supreme Court of India has ruled that women in live-in relationships can seek protection under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalises cruelty by a husband or his relatives toward a married woman. The landmark judgment settles a legal question that had divided high courts and lower courts for years: whether the word "husband" in the anti-cruelty provision can extend to a man who cohabits with a woman in a relationship resembling marriage.

A bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Nongmeikapam Kotiswar Singh delivered the ruling in Lokesh B.H. and Others v. State of Karnataka, a case that originated from a domestic cruelty complaint filed by a woman in Bengaluru. The complainant alleged that her partner — who had concealed a prior subsisting marriage — harassed her and attempted to set her on fire over dowry demands.

The Legal Question at the Heart of the Case

Section 498A IPC, introduced in 1983, was designed as a social reform measure to combat dowry harassment and domestic cruelty against married women. It prescribes imprisonment of up to three years and a fine. The provision's language specifically refers to "husband or relative of husband," raising the question of whether it covers partners in relationships that fall outside the strict definition of a legal marriage.

The accused in the case, Lokesh B.H., argued that because he had a prior valid marriage, any subsequent union with the complainant was void ab initio. At best, he contended, the arrangement was a live-in relationship — placing it outside Section 498A's reach.

"The term 'husband' in Section 498A must be given a purposive and expansive construction, and the protection afforded by the provision cannot be denied merely on the technical ground of a void marriage."

— Karnataka High Court, in its November 2025 judgment upheld by the Supreme Court

The Karnataka High Court, in a judgment by Justice Suraj Govindaraj dated November 18, 2025, had rejected this argument. The Supreme Court agreed, holding that interpreting "husband" narrowly would defeat the provision's protective purpose and leave vulnerable women without legal recourse.

Impact on India's Legal Landscape

The ruling carries significance beyond the individual case. India has no standalone law governing live-in relationships, and legal protections for cohabiting partners have developed unevenly. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 already extends certain economic rights and civil remedies to women in "relationships in the nature of marriage." But the criminal law dimension — whether live-in partners face prosecution for cruelty under Section 498A — had remained unsettled at the Supreme Court level.

The court's decision also has implications for Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, which replaced Section 498A when the new criminal code took effect. Section 85 retains the same language referring to "husband or relative of husband," meaning the Supreme Court's expansive interpretation will apply to cases under the new law as well.

The Union of India was impleaded as a party in the case, with Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati assisting the court. Prominent advocate Nina R. Nariman was appointed amicus curiae, reflecting the significance the bench attached to the legal question.

A Growing Social Reality

India's 2021 census data and subsequent surveys have documented a steady rise in live-in relationships, particularly in urban centres. While the practice remains a small fraction of total partnerships, its growth has outpaced the evolution of legal frameworks designed for traditional marriages. Courts across India have grappled with where live-in partners fit within statutes drafted decades ago.

The Supreme Court's ruling is consistent with a broader judicial trend of recognising the substantive character of domestic relationships over their formal legal status. In recent years, courts have held that long-term cohabitation may create presumptions of marriage for maintenance claims under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

"Where a man induces a woman to believe that she is lawfully married to him, and thereafter subjects her to cruelty, such a man cannot be permitted to evade criminal responsibility on the plea that no valid marriage existed in law."

— Karnataka High Court, Justice Suraj Govindaraj

Looking Ahead

The ruling is expected to prompt an increase in domestic cruelty complaints from women in live-in arrangements. Legal practitioners note that the decision still requires the complainant to demonstrate that the relationship bore essential characteristics of marriage — mere casual cohabitation may not meet the threshold. The court emphasised that the factual allegations must satisfy the elements of "cruelty" as defined in the explanation to Section 498A.

For the Indian diaspora, the judgment is relevant to NRIs and OCIs navigating relationships across jurisdictions. Indian courts have increasingly asserted jurisdiction over domestic cruelty complaints filed by women whose partners reside abroad, and the expanded definition of "husband" under 498A could apply to cross-border live-in arrangements as well.
